mcqs.question: A pre-attention encoder-decoder RNN translates short sentences well but degrades sharply on long ones. What is the root cause?
options: The entire input must be compressed into one fixed-size context vector, and information from early tokens gets diluted by the time the encoder reaches the end of a long sentence
The decoder has too few parameters to generate long output sequences
RNNs cannot process sequences longer than their training examples at all
The vocabulary size is too small to cover long sentences
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic seq2seq bottleneck: the decoder only ever sees the encoder's final fixed-size hidden state, so as sentence length grows, early information gets progressively overwritten before the decoder can use it. It isn't a parameter-count or vocabulary issue (A, D), and RNNs can technically process longer sequences than seen in training, just with degrading quality (C is overstated).

mcqs.question: In "the trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", attention correctly resolves "it" to "trophy". Which part of the query/key/value mechanism directly produces this result?
options: The value vectors alone, since they store the final word meanings
"It"'s query vector scores highly against "trophy"'s key vector (high dot-product similarity), giving "trophy"'s value a large weight in the softmax-weighted sum
A hard-coded coreference-resolution rule inserted before the attention layer
The positional encoding of "it", since it happens to be near the end of the sentence
mcqs.explanation: Attention resolves the reference purely through learned query-key similarity: "it"'s query is compared against every key, and if "trophy"'s key produces a high dot product, softmax assigns it a large weight, so "it"'s output is dominated by "trophy"'s value. There's no hard-coded rule (C); position alone doesn't resolve semantic reference (D); and values alone, without the query-key scoring step, wouldn't know which value to weight most (A).

mcqs.question: Why does a Transformer use 8 or 12 attention heads instead of one larger single-head attention computation?
options: A single attention head cannot mathematically process sequences longer than one token
Multiple heads are required purely to parallelize computation across GPUs
Multiple heads let different subspaces specialize in different relationship types (e.g. syntax vs coreference), increasing representational diversity rather than raw computation
More heads directly increase the model's total attention computation, at the cost of speed, for no representational benefit
mcqs.explanation: Multi-head attention runs several smaller attention computations in parallel subspaces so different heads can specialize (one might track subject-verb agreement, another coreference), improving representational richness — each head works in a smaller dimension so total compute is comparable to one large head, not simply "more of the same" (contradicting D). GPU parallelism (B) is a side benefit, not the reason for the design, and single-head attention works fine on multi-token sequences (C is false).

mcqs.question: If you removed positional encoding entirely from a Transformer, what would happen to its ability to distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog"?
options: No change — self-attention inherently tracks word order via the sequence of the attention computation
It would only affect the decoder, not the encoder
The model would still distinguish them, but only for sentences longer than 10 tokens
The model would attend to the token embeddings identically regardless of order, since self-attention's pairwise scoring has no built-in notion of position
mcqs.explanation: Self-attention computes pairwise scores based purely on content (query/key similarity), with no inherent sense of position — feed it the same set of tokens in a different order and, absent positional encoding, the set of pairwise interactions is unchanged. That's exactly why positional encoding must be added to the input embeddings before attention runs. There's no length threshold (C) and both encoder and decoder self-attention are equally order-blind without it (D is wrong).

mcqs.question: Why do Transformer blocks wrap each sub-layer (attention, feedforward) with a residual connection before stacking dozens of them?
options: They let gradients flow directly back through many stacked layers during backpropagation, avoiding the vanishing-gradient problem that deep stacks would otherwise suffer
Residual connections reduce the total parameter count of the model
They are required only for encoder-decoder models, not encoder-only or decoder-only ones
They replace the need for layer normalization entirely
mcqs.explanation: Residual (skip) connections add each sub-layer's input directly to its output, giving gradients a direct path through the stack instead of having to flow through every nonlinear transformation, which is essential once you stack 12–96+ blocks. They don't reduce parameter count (A is false — they add none but don't remove any either), apply equally to all three architecture families (C is wrong), and are used alongside layer norm, not instead of it (D is wrong).

mcqs.question: You need a model for machine translation, where the input (source language) and output (target language) are genuinely different sequences of different lengths. Which architecture family fits best, and why?
options: Encoder-only, because bidirectional context is all that's needed
Encoder-decoder, because the encoder builds a full bidirectional representation of the source while the decoder generates the target, cross-attending to that representation
Decoder-only, because generation only ever needs causal masking
Any of the three families perform identically on sequence-to-sequence tasks
mcqs.explanation: Encoder-decoder architectures exist precisely for this case: the encoder can see the whole source sentence bidirectionally (no need to mask, since it's not generating), while the decoder generates the target autoregressively and cross-attends back to the encoder's output. Encoder-only models (A) have no generation mechanism at all; decoder-only models (B) can be prompted for translation but lack a dedicated bidirectional encoding pass over the source; the three families are not interchangeable (D is false).

mcqs.question: Training an LSTM and a Transformer of comparable size on the same large dataset, the Transformer finishes training noticeably faster on the same GPU cluster. What is the primary architectural reason?
options: Transformers have fewer total parameters than LSTMs of comparable capacity
Transformers use a smaller vocabulary, reducing compute per step

LSTMs must process tokens sequentially step-by-step, which prevents parallelizing computation across the time dimension; Transformer self-attention processes all positions simultaneously as matrix operations
LSTMs require more attention heads, which slows training
mcqs.explanation: The core throughput difference is parallelism: an LSTM's hidden state at step t depends on step t-1, forcing sequential computation across time; a Transformer computes attention for all token pairs in one matrix multiplication, fully parallelizable across positions. Parameter count (A) isn't inherently smaller, vocabulary size (C) is independent of architecture choice, and LSTMs don't use attention heads at all (D is a category error).

mcqs.question: A team doubles their Transformer's context window from 2,048 to 4,096 tokens and is surprised training slows by roughly 4x rather than 2x. What explains this?
options: This is unexpected and indicates a bug, since attention cost should scale linearly with sequence length
The team must have also doubled the number of layers
Tokenizer vocabulary size scales with context window length
Self-attention cost scales quadratically with sequence length, so doubling the length roughly quadruples the pairwise score computations
mcqs.explanation: Self-attention computes a score for every pair of tokens, so cost is O(n²) in sequence length — doubling n roughly quadruples the number of pairwise scores, matching the observed slowdown. This isn't a bug (D is wrong) and has nothing to do with layer count (B) or vocabulary size (C, which is independent of context length).
